entries.definition: Appearance or luminosity. Munidatta pairs a moon-appearance and a sun-appearance, which he equates with the grasped and the grasper (cp.14.m2), and speaks of three appearances, the moon, the sun and the pulinda, which make and unmake saṃsāra and which practice stops (cp.14.m5).

The higher knowledges: extraordinary capacities that Buddhist texts ascribe to advanced practitioners, usually six (magical powers, the divine ear, knowing others' minds, recalling past lives, the divine eye, and the ending of the defilements). Munidatta says the poet raised his mark to display them (cp.04.m6).

A tantric rite by which a teacher admits a disciple to a practice. Munidatta describes a yogin, consecrated in due order and having pleased the true guru with offerings of pledge substances, receiving the wisdom-knowledge empowerment at midnight (cp.01.m3).

Nondual, nonduality (advaya): the absence of two, as of subject and object or of wisdom and means, a key word of the siddhas. Line 3b opens with ādaadiṭi, whose first part may stand for advaya, though the division is uncertain; Munidatta's gloss has 'coupled union' (yuganaddha) and the Tibetan 'two' (gnyis).

forms.translit: rgas pa dang 'chi ba nyid med pa

entries.definition: Free from old age and death (Sanskrit ajarāmara): a body that neither ages nor dies, a goal shared by the siddhas' yoga and Indian alchemy. The refrain of song 3 speaks of becoming ageless and deathless; Munidatta says this is gained through a special practice once bodhicitta is bound with the noose of imperishable bliss (cp.03.m3).

Imperishable or unchanging bliss: bliss that does not decline because the vital essence is not lost (akṣara, ‘not flowing away’); the term is central in the Kālacakra tradition. Munidatta says bodhicitta gone to self-blessing is bound with the noose of the bliss of imperishability (cp.03.m3); the Tibetan has mi 'gyur ba'i bde ba, ‘unchanging bliss’.

The series of Sanskrit vowels. Munidatta glosses the dhamaṇa of song 1 as āli, with the purification of the moon, and quotes the Dvikalpa: the union of āli and kāli is Vajrasattva's seat (cp.01.m6). In song 7 Munidatta reads the pair differently: āli with (ā)lokajñāna and kāli with (ā)lokābhāsa, apparently the light and the spreading of light of the completion stage (cp.07.m2); the Tibetan there has 'jigs byed and dus mtshan ma.

Light (āloka): in the Guhyasamāja completion stage, the first of three ever subtler luminous experiences (light, spreading of light, culmination of light) in which the winds and concepts dissolve. Munidatta glosses the song's āli as lokajñāna (cp.07.m2); the Tibetan, ye shes kyi snang ba, suggests reading ālokajñāna, 'the knowledge that is light'.

Spreading of light (ālokābhāsa): in the Guhyasamāja completion stage, the second of three ever subtler luminous experiences, following light (āloka). Munidatta glosses the song's kāli as lokabhāsa (cp.07.m2); the Tibetan has snang ba mched pa, 'increase of appearance', the usual rendering of ālokābhāsa.

Joy. The tantras Munidatta cites count four joys arising in yogic union; the order of the last two, the joy of cessation (viramānanda) and innate joy (sahajānanda), differs between systems. Munidatta calls great bliss 'the fourth joy' and speaks of knowing innate joy in the joy of cessation (cp.01.m3).

An embrace (Sanskrit aṅkapālī; aṅka is 'lap' or 'flank'), which the poet asks the yoginī to give. Munidatta explains the word as if it were aṅka, 'mark', and pāl-, 'protect'. The Tibetan translation has yan lag 'khyud, 'embrace of the limbs'.

symbolic.image: the embrace the poet asks the yoginī to give

readings.referent: she gives her own mark (aṅka, svacihna) to the practitioner and protects it (pālayati)
or else, through union marked by the moments beginning with vicitra, she gives the sequence of joys

entries.definition: The two sides or edges (Old Bengali duānte, 'at both ends'): in song 5, the two banks of the river of existence, both muddy. Munidatta renders it antadvaya and explains it as the near and far banks, left and right. Sanskrit anta and Tibetan mtha' also mean 'extreme', as in the two extremes the Middle Way avoids.

symbolic.image: the two muddy sides of the river

readings.referent: the near and far banks (pārāvāra), left and right, smeared with the mud of the faults of nature

entries.definition: The existence between death and the next birth, which many Buddhist schools say a being passes through before rebirth. In a scriptural verse Munidatta quotes, it is named with arising, abiding and ceasing, and all conceptual thought is called the work of wind and mind (cp.04.m3).

Non-apprehension (anupalambha): finding nothing to take as an object, since nothing exists by its own nature; a Madhyamaka term. Munidatta speaks of the non-apprehension of all things, with grasped and grasper absent (cp.06.m2). The manuscript's anulambha is apparently a slip: the Tibetan dmigs su med pa supports anupalambha.

Midnight (Old Bengali adharātī, Sanskrit ardharātri, 'half of the night'). In the refrain of song 2 the thief takes the earring at midnight. Munidatta sets it beside 'the fourth juncture' (caturthī sandhyā); the empowerment entry records a midnight empowerment in his comment on song 1.

symbolic.image: midnight, when the thief takes the earring

readings.referent: the fourth juncture (caturthī sandhyā), named in apposition to midnight: the time, in the house of the avadhūtī of the joy of cessation, when the thief, innate joy, steals the 'wealth' of the faults of the winds

entries.definition: The name of the rāga (melodic mode) to which song 4 is sung, given in its heading. The Tibetan translation calls the melody skya rengs, 'dawn', as if the name were Sanskrit aruṇa, 'dawn-red'; whether aru is a shortened form of that word is uncertain.

The eight powers that Indian yoga traditions ascribe to accomplished yogis, such as becoming minute, becoming light, and lordship over others. Munidatta names them as part of the mark of the lord of yogis that the poet raises (cp.04.m6); the Tibetan has 'the eight qualities, beginning with lordship'.

forms.where: standard Tibetan equivalent; not checked against toh2293

entries.definition: Literally ‘she who has shaken off’: in tantric yoga, the central channel of the subtle body, running between a left and a right channel, into which the yogin draws the vital energies. Munidatta distinguishes a purified avadhūtī, which he equates with Nairātmā, from an unpurified one.

Ignorance: the basic misapprehension of how things are, which Buddhist teaching places at the root of saṃsāra as the first link of dependent arising. In song 10 Munidatta says the lotus-place has the form of ignorance.

An axe (Old Bengali ṭāṅgī; compare Sanskrit ṭaṅka, 'axe, chisel'), used in song 5 in building the bridge. Munidatta's gloss has paraśu, 'axe'. The Tibetan translation of the line has gzong gnyis, 'two chisels'; its comment has sta re, 'axe'.

symbolic.image: the axe used in building the bridge

readings.referent: the axe of coupled union (yuganaddha), with which the work is made firm in order to show its fruit

entries.definition: Bark (Sanskrit valkala). In song 3 the liquor-seller uses fine bark to make her liquor; a fermenting starter made from bark, roots and herbs may be what is meant. The Tibetan translation has phabs, ‘yeast’, in this line (cp.03.1b).

The female organ (the word also means ‘good fortune, share’), a frequent term in the yoginī tantras and their commentaries. Munidatta equates the cord Ḍombī sells with the bhaga, ‘the place of the lotus’, which he says has the form of ignorance (cp.10.m6).

Existence or becoming (bhava): the round of repeated birth, often a synonym of saṃsāra and set against nirvāṇa. Song 5 opens with the river of existence (bhavaṇai). In the verse of Saraha that Munidatta quotes, bhava stands beside nirvāṇa (cp.05.m3). The Tibetan has srid pa.

A word of uncertain sense, addressed in the vocative in the refrain of song 2 ('listen, O biātī'). The Tibetan translation renders it rigs ngan, 'low-born woman', which suggests Sanskrit vijātī, 'of other (low) birth'; other derivations are possible. Munidatta writes viātī.

symbolic.image: the woman addressed as biātī in the refrain

readings.referent: the purified avadhūtī, which the lord of yogis, having resolved on its form in himself, addresses: 'O purified avadhūtī, listen'

entries.definition: A drop: in tantric yoga, a drop of the vital essence, bodhicitta, which in its bodily form is semen and is guarded and moved through the channels of the subtle body. Munidatta speaks of the drop of bodhicitta at the opening in the tip of the vajra-jewel (cp.03.m2).
A river boat, one of the commonest images of the songs, with its ferryman, oars and crossings. In this song Kāṇha asks Ḍombī in whose boat she comes and goes.

symbolic.image: the boat in which Ḍombī comes and goes

readings.referent: the path of conventional bodhicitta, on which she comes and goes (he adds that in fact she does not)
what lies in the middle: the channel of semen (śukranāḍikā) in the avadhūtī of the joy of cessation (the syntax of the gloss is loose)
the path of the joy of cessation, purified by the innate
purified bodhicitta, which the yogī is told to row

entries.definition: Awakening (bodhi): the realization that makes one a buddha. In song 5 the poet says awakening is near and one should not go far. Munidatta speaks of the accomplishment of bodhi-Mahāmudrā, very near through practice (cp.05.m5). In the last line the Tibetan translation has byang chub, 'awakening', where the Bengali has 'lord'.

forms.where: standard Tibetan equivalent; not checked against toh2293

forms.translit: kun rdzob byang chub kyi sems

entries.definition: 'Mind of awakening'. In the Mahāyāna, the resolve to reach awakening for all beings; in the tantras also a subtle bodily essence whose loss must be prevented. Munidatta speaks of 'the moon of conventional bodhicitta' drying up, and quotes the Rativajra: once bodhicitta has fallen, how can there be flawless accomplishment? (cp.01.m2).
A string of bone beads or carved bone ornaments, part of the regalia of kāpālika ascetics and tantric yogis. Kāṇha says he has put one on for Ḍombī's sake.

symbolic.image: a garland of bones

entries.definition: A member of the priestly caste at the head of the caste order, bound by rules of ritual purity that forbid contact with untouchables. The first couplet of this song sets a shaven-headed brahmin beside Ḍombī's hut outside the town.

symbolic.image: a shaven-headed brahmin

readings.referent: the mind as a restless young brahmin (cittavaṭuka, ‘mind-lad’), born from the seed syllable HŪṂ called brahma

entries.definition: A young wife living in her husband's family home (Old Bengali bahuṛī, from Sanskrit vadhūṭī); the Tibetan translation has mna' ma, 'bride, daughter-in-law'. In song 2 she stays awake while her father-in-law sleeps, is afraid by day, and goes to Kāmaru at night.

symbolic.image: the young wife of the household

readings.referent: the yoginīs, in the form of the naturally purified avadhūtī, who keep awake day and night

the avadhūtī, which in its conventional aspect, as semen, creates the three worlds and then, producing the knowledge of day, is afraid; at night, as the naturally purified avadhūtī, it empowers the five aggregates and goes of itself, free of concepts, to its own place in the wheel of great bliss

entries.definition: A bridge or crossing (Old Bengali sāṅkama, Sanskrit saṃkrama). In the refrain of song 5 Cāṭila builds a bridge over the river of existence, from the planks of a split tree, so that people bound for the far shore can cross; whoever climbs onto it is not to go right or left.

symbolic.image: the bridge Cāṭila builds over the river of existence

readings.referent: the unity of self-blessing (svādhiṣṭhāna) and clear light (prabhāsvara), the Jina's bridge for carrying beings across the ocean of saṃsāra; the Sanskrit reads sthādhiṣṭhāna, evidently for svādhiṣṭhāna, as the Tibetan rang byin gyis brlab pa confirms
the unity of the conventional and the ultimate, which Cāṭila joins through the guru's lineage; the Sanskrit word glossed here, śatrumam, looks corrupt, and the Tibetan has zam pa, 'bridge'

entries.definition: A word of uncertain literal sense in the last line of song 1, paired with dhamaṇa; the two appear as the seat on which the poet sits. It may be related to Sanskrit camana, 'sipping'. Munidatta spells it cavaṇa.

symbolic.image: camaṇa, one of the pair that serves as the poet's seat

readings.referent: kāli, the consonant series, with the purification of the sun

forms.where: standard Tibetan equivalent; not checked against toh2293

entries.definition: Tantric conduct: the outward way of life of an adept, including dress, ornaments, song and behaviour that defies convention. The word gives the Caryāgīti, ‘songs of conduct’, their name. Munidatta speaks here of conduct ‘with elaboration’ (saprapañca).

A sign or mark (Sanskrit cihna). In song 3 a sign is seen at the tenth door and a customer comes, perhaps like the sign that advertised a liquor shop. Munidatta speaks of the sign of the delight of the bliss of great passion seen at the door of Vairocana (cp.03.m4). The Tibetan translation has rtags.

symbolic.image: a sign seen at the tenth door

readings.referent: the sign of the delight of the bliss of great passion (mahārāgasukhapramodacihna), which the gandharva being sees at the door of Vairocana before it enters

entries.definition: Mud or mire (Old Bengali cikhila), which in song 5 lies on both sides of the river of existence. Munidatta repeats the word and explains it with paṅka, 'mud'. The Tibetan translation has rab 'dred, 'very slippery', in the line and in the comment.

symbolic.image: mud on both sides of the river

readings.referent: the mud of the faults of nature (prakṛtidoṣa) with which the two banks, near and far, left and right, are smeared; the Tibetan translation instead has 'not stained by the mud of the faults of nature' and applies it to the middle

entries.definition: A strip of cloth or rag (Sanskrit cīra), here raised like a flag: the poet says he has raised it among men and women. The Tibetan translation renders it rtags mtshan, 'sign, emblem'.

symbolic.image: the cloth the poet raises among men and women

readings.referent: the mark of the lord of yogis (yogīndracihna), the eightfold mastery and the rest, raised to display the higher knowledges

forbiddenInLine: mark of the lord of yogis

entries.definition: Mind: the stream of thought and awareness. Song 1 speaks of the restless mind. In a verse Munidatta quotes, the mind clouded by concepts, restless as windblown lightning and stained by passion is called saṃsāra (cp.01.m2).

Coming and going (Old Bengali abaṇāgabaṇa, apparently a pair of verbal nouns; compare Sanskrit āgamana, gamana). In song 7 Kāṇha is downcast 'in coming and going', after the couplet on whatever came and went. The Tibetan translation seems to parse the word differently, as bdag nyid 'ongs nas, 'having come himself'.

symbolic.image: coming and going

readings.referent: the arising and perishing (utpāda, bhaṅga) of things, in which, knowing the nature of conventional truth by the guru's grace, Kṛṣṇācārya becomes of distinguished mind (the paraphrase puts utpādabhaṅgeṣu where the song has abaṇāgabaṇe; there is no explicit gloss)

entries.definition: The open yard of a house (Sanskrit aṅgana), the first word of the refrain of song 2. The Tibetan commentary has sgo mdun, 'in front of the door'; its quotation of the song reads sgo bdun, 'seven doors', probably a slip for the same words.

symbolic.image: the courtyard of the house, in the refrain

readings.referent: the wind of emergence (vyutthāna) and entering; the wording of the gloss is obscure, and the Tibetan has 'entering, with reference to the wind of arising'

entries.definition: A crocodile (Sanskrit kumbhīra, the broad-snouted crocodile of Indian rivers); the Tibetan translation has chu srin, a water monster. In song 2 it eats the tamarind of a tree. Munidatta reads it through kumbhaka, breath retention, a word it resembles.

symbolic.image: a crocodile that eats the tamarind of the tree

readings.referent: the absorption of kumbhaka (breath retention) purified by vilakṣaṇa, which, with the stages of one's own experience, 'eats' bodhicitta, that is, makes it without intrinsic nature

entries.definition: What the young wife fears by day in song 2. The rendering 'crow' rests on the Tibetan translation, which has bya rog, 'crow', in the song and the commentary; the Old Bengali kāṛai is otherwise uncertain and might be parsed differently. Munidatta quotes the word without a Sanskrit equivalent.

symbolic.image: the crow the young wife fears by day

readings.referent: the kāyakālapuruṣa, the 'Man of Time' of the body (Tibetan dus kyi skyes bu, 'person of time'), of whom she is afraid and terrified

entries.definition: The tenth door or opening of the body: yogic traditions count nine bodily openings and add a hidden tenth, often placed at the crown of the head. In song 3 a sign is seen at the tenth door. Munidatta calls it the door of Vairocana (cp.03.m4).

symbolic.image: the tenth door, at which a sign is seen

readings.referent: the door of Vairocana (vairocanadvāra), where the sign of the delight of the bliss of great passion is seen, and by which the gandharva being enters

entries.definition: A deer or antelope (Old Bengali hariṇā, Sanskrit hariṇa, mṛga), the central figure of this song: its own flesh makes it an enemy, it touches neither grass nor water, and its hooves are not seen as it bounds away. Munidatta says the poet speaks in the twilight language of the word 'deer' (cp.06.m1), and calls it 'the mind-deer' throughout.

symbolic.image: a deer, an enemy through its own flesh, that touches neither grass nor water and whose hooves are not seen as it bounds away

readings.referent: the mind, which Munidatta calls 'the mind-deer' (cittahariṇa) throughout his comment
with the doe, the pair 'mind and wind' (cittapavana), whose dwelling is not understood through the door of the senses (the gloss does not say which animal is which)

entries.definition: Meditation in which practitioners visualize themselves as the deity of a tantra, the foundation of tantric practice. Munidatta says the lord of yogis first makes firm the vajra of body, beginning with deity yoga (cp.04.m5).

A word of uncertain literal sense in the last line of song 1, paired with camaṇa; the two appear as the seat on which the poet sits. It may be related to Sanskrit dhamana, 'blowing'. Munidatta spells it dhavana.

symbolic.image: dhamaṇa, one of the pair that serves as the poet's seat

readings.referent: āli, the vowel series, with the purification of the moon

entries.definition: Dharma: the Buddha's teaching, and also any phenomenon. In song 5 Cāṭila builds the bridge for the sake of dharma. Munidatta takes the word as 'phenomenon': a dharma holds its own characteristic, like a pot or a cloth, and has no form by its own nature (cp.05.m3). The Tibetan of the line has chos dbyings, 'sphere of phenomena'.

The heaps or sections (skandha) of the Buddha's teaching, traditionally counted as eighty-four thousand; skandha here does not mean the five aggregates. In the tantra verse Munidatta quotes, the Sage's eighty-four thousand heaps of Dharma bear no fruit for those who do not know reality (cp.06.m6).

The refrain of a song, usually its second couplet, sung again after each later couplet. Munidatta names it when commenting on it. The abbreviation ধ্রু in Shastri's edition is only a cue to repeat the refrain and is not translated.

A code word of the twilight language. In the Hevajra verse Munidatta quotes, the unfit (abhavya) is called ḍiṇḍima and the fit 'great kāliñjara' (cp.04.m3). As an ordinary word a ḍiṇḍima is a kind of drum.

symbolic.image: ḍiṇḍima, in ordinary use a kind of drum

readings.referent: the unfit (abhavya)
readings.per: the Hevajra Tantra, as quoted by Munidatta

entries.definition: A doe, the female deer (Old Bengali hariṇī). In this song her dwelling (or that of the pair) is not known, and she tells the deer to leave this forest. Munidatta calls hariṇī twilight language for the wisdom seal (jñānamudrā), Nairātmā, and derives the word from harati, 'takes away' (cp.06.m5). The Tibetan translation has ri dgas ma.

symbolic.image: the doe, who tells the deer to leave this forest

readings.referent: the wisdom seal (jñānamudrā), Nairātmā: hariṇī is twilight language for her, 'she who takes away' (harati) the graspings of existence; as the meditator's practice matures she comforts the mind-deer and tells it to leave the body-forest for the lotus grove of great bliss
with the deer, the pair 'mind and wind' (cittapavana), whose dwelling is not understood through the door of the senses; the gloss implies that the doe is the wind but does not say so

entries.definition: A woman of the Ḍom caste, a community that caste society treated as untouchable and kept at the edge of towns and villages. In Kāṇha's songs she is the woman the poet addresses and desires; in this song her hut stands outside the town, she dances on a lotus, and he says he will kill her.

symbolic.image: a Ḍom woman whose hut stands outside the town

readings.referent: Nairātmā (selflessness as a goddess), the purified avadhūtī; she is called Ḍombī because she cannot be touched
Nairātmā, whom he addresses in place of Ḍombī (‘O Ḍombī, Nairātmā’)
the unpurified avadhūtī, for one who lacks the guru's lineage

forms.where: standard Tibetan equivalent; not checked against toh2293

entries.definition: ‘One taste’: the realization that all things share a single nature, so that apparent opposites are not experienced as separate; a key term of siddha and Mahāmudrā teaching. Munidatta says Kṛṣṇācārya dances on the lotus with Nairātmā ‘in one taste’.

An elephant, one of the recurring images of siddha poetry. In the verse of Kṛṣṇācārya's Dohākoṣa that Munidatta quotes, the great elephant (karivara) dwells far away (cp.06.m4); Munidatta does not explain the images of the verse. The Tibetan translation has glang chen mchog, 'best of elephants'.

The syllables e and vaṃ, which open the formula ‘Thus (evaṃ) have I heard’ at the head of the sūtras and tantras; in the yoginī tantras they stand for the female and male, wisdom and means, joined. In a verse of Kāṇha that Munidatta quotes, the lotus blossoms taking evaṃkāra as its seed (cp.03.m4).

The husband's father (Old Bengali susurā, Sanskrit śvaśura), who in song 2 falls asleep while the young wife stays awake. The Tibetan translation has sgyug mo, 'mother-in-law', both in the song and in the commentary. Munidatta cites the word as sasurā.

symbolic.image: the father-in-law who has fallen asleep

readings.referent: the breath, beginning with the 'swift' (tvarita), led into yogic sleep, the fourth joy

entries.definition: A forest or wood (Old Bengali baṇa, Sanskrit vana). In this song the doe tells the deer to leave this forest. Munidatta reads it as the body, 'this body-forest' (kāyavana) (cp.06.m5). The Tibetan translation has nags, 'forest', in the line and lus kyi nags, 'forest of the body', in the commentary.

symbolic.image: this forest, which the doe tells the deer to leave

readings.referent: the body, 'this body-forest' (kāyavana): the mind-deer is to give up its grasping at the body (kāyagraha) and go to the lotus grove of great bliss

entries.definition: Sky; open space. The sky is a common image in siddha poetry and in Buddhist tantric language. In this song it forms the first half of gaaṇadukhola, the vessel used to bail the boat; Munidatta repeats the compound (gaganadukholaka) without explaining it.

symbolic.image: the sky, in the compound 'sky-scoop' used to bail the boat

entries.definition: In Buddhist doctrine, the being of the intermediate state between death and rebirth, said to feed on smells and to enter the womb at conception; in Indian myth also a celestial musician. Munidatta reads the song's customer as the gandharva being (gandharvasattva), who enters by the door of Vairocana and does not come out (cp.03.m4, cp.03.m6).

A buyer or customer (Sanskrit grāhaka, a word that also means ‘grasper’). In song 3 a customer comes to the liquor-seller, and one who has gone in does not come out. The Tibetan translation renders ‘beer-buyer’ (chang nyo) and ‘beer-drinker’ (chang 'thung).

symbolic.image: a customer who comes to the liquor shop and, once inside, does not come out

readings.referent: the gandharva being (gandharvasattva), who, seeing the sign of the delight of the bliss of great passion at the door of Vairocana, comes of itself, enters by that door and drinks the juice of the lotus of great bliss

the gandharva being, which enters from the blazing fire of great passion and whose entry has no coming out; Munidatta calls this couplet the stopping of the gandharva being's going (the comment survives only in the Tibetan translation)

entries.definition: Gavaṛā, the name of the rāga (melodic mode) to which song 2 is sung, given in its heading. The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) instead names the melody chen po, 'great'; why it does so is unclear.

The pair 'what is grasped' and 'what grasps', object and subject. Buddhist thought, especially Yogācāra and the tantras, treats their apparent separation as the root of delusion. Munidatta applies the pair to the Gaṅgā and the Yamunā, and says Nairātmā accepts nothing in the manner of grasped and grasper.

Guñjarī, the name of the rāga (melodic mode) to which song 5 is sung, given in its heading. The Tibetan translation transcribes it gu dz+dza rI, which may point to Gujjarī, a Prakrit form of the rāga name Gurjarī; how the two spellings relate is uncertain.

A spiritual teacher. The refrain of song 1 tells the listener to ask the guru. Munidatta stresses that empowerment and the key instruction come from the true guru, and quotes the Guhyasamāja: without the vajra guru one cannot reach nirvāṇa (cp.01.m3).

The unbroken transmission of practical instruction from teacher to student in tantric practice. Munidatta says Ḍombī's hut is known through it, and that for one who lacks it Ḍombī is the unpurified avadhūtī.

A hoof (Old Bengali khūra, Sanskrit khura). In the last couplet the deer's hooves are not seen as it bounds away; the Tibetan translation has rkang, 'foot, leg'. Munidatta's paraphrase puts 'the parts and so on' of the mind-deer in their place: yogis who have realized innate knowledge form no concepts of them (cp.06.m6).

symbolic.image: the deer's hooves, not seen as it bounds away

readings.referent: the parts (avayava) and so on of one's own mind-deer, of which yogis who have realized innate knowledge form no concepts (his paraphrase puts them where the song has the hooves; he gives no explicit gloss)

entries.definition: A house or home (Old Bengali ghara, Sanskrit gṛha; Tibetan khang, khyim). In song 2 the refrain's gharapaṇa is not clearly segmented: ghara, "house", with an uncertain second element, is assumed. In song 3 the one liquor-seller is in two houses; in the verse of Kāṇha that Munidatta quotes, the motionless wind stays in the house of the housewife.

symbolic.image: the house of the refrain, where the thief comes at midnight; the two houses of the one liquor-seller

readings.referent: the house of the avadhūtī of the joy of cessation (viramānandāvadhūtīgṛha), to which the lord of yogis is told first to lead both by the instruction in vajra recitation; the gloss does not quote the song's word
the moon and the sun, left and right, which are joined and made to enter the middle channel; Munidatta glosses ‘the two’ without repeating the word ‘house’

entries.definition: A small dwelling of thatch, bamboo or mud. In this song it is Ḍombī's hut, standing outside the town.

symbolic.image: Ḍombī's hut outside the town

readings.referent: the wheel of great bliss (mahāsukhacakra), beyond the reach of the senses and known through the guru's lineage (he calls it ‘your house’, tavāgāra)

entries.definition: The senses or sense faculties (indriya): eye, ear, nose, tongue and body, with the mind in some lists, each a 'door' through which objects are known. Munidatta says the dwelling of the mind and the wind is not understood through the door of the senses (cp.06.m4).

'The city of the Jina' (the Victor, a title of the Buddha): the place the singer says he will reach again through the true guru. The Old Bengali jiṇaurā corresponds to Sanskrit jinapura, the form Munidatta uses.

symbolic.image: the city of the Jina, the goal of the crossing

readings.referent: the city of great bliss (mahāsukhapura)

entries.definition: 'Wisdom seal': in the yoginī tantras, a partner visualized in meditation, as distinct from a physical partner (karmamudrā) and from Mahāmudrā. Munidatta says hariṇī, 'doe', is twilight language for the jñānamudrā, Nairātmā, who comforts the mind-deer as the meditator's practice matures (cp.06.m5).
A cowrie shell, used as small change in eastern India. In the song the ferrywoman takes no cowrie for the crossing; Munidatta compares the ordinary ferry-master, who takes a cowrie as the fare.

Kāla, 'time', and by extension death: time as the destroyer. In song 1 it enters the restless mind. Munidatta identifies it with Rāhu, the eclipse demon, and supports this with a verse of Kṛṣṇācārya in which the pure water dries up when the fire of time (kālāgni) enters (cp.01.m2).

symbolic.image: Kāla, time or death, entering the restless mind

readings.referent: Rāhu, who from the first day of the dark fortnight dries up the moon of conventional bodhicitta through the sequence of lunar days

entries.definition: 'The Man of Time': time personified, or a servant of Yama, lord of the dead. Munidatta says the young wife fears the kāyakālapuruṣa, perhaps 'the Man of Time in the body' (the compound is unclear), glossing the word the Tibetan translation takes as 'crow' (cp.02.m5).

The series of Sanskrit consonants. Munidatta glosses the camaṇa of song 1 as kāli, with the purification of the sun, and quotes the union of āli and kāli as Vajrasattva's seat (cp.01.m6). In song 7 he pairs it instead with (ā)lokābhāsa, the spreading of light, as āli with the light (cp.07.m2). Not to be confused with kāla or the goddess Kālī.

A code word of the twilight language. In the Hevajra verse Munidatta quotes, the fit (bhavya) is called 'great kāliñjara' and the unfit ḍiṇḍima (cp.04.m3); in his own sentence the Tibetan translation renders the word by its sense, skal ba dang ldan pa, 'fortunate'. As an ordinary name, Kāliñjara is a hill fort in central India.

symbolic.image: kāliñjara, in ordinary use the name of a hill fort

readings.referent: the fit (bhavya)
readings.per: the Hevajra Tantra, as quoted by Munidatta

entries.definition: The juice or nectar (rasa) of the lotus, which the poet says he drinks after kissing the yoginī's mouth. The Tibetan translation has chu skyes khu ba, 'lotus juice'.

symbolic.image: the lotus nectar the poet drinks after kissing the yoginī's mouth

readings.referent: ultimate (paramārtha) bodhicitta, described as the intoxicating honey of the uṣṇīṣa lotus

entries.definition: An object the thief takes at midnight, apparently an ear ornament (Old Bengali kāna, 'ear'), though the literal sense is not certain and Munidatta does not give it. The Tibetan translation has mdo phugs khang logs, which seems to describe a part of the house rather than an ornament.

symbolic.image: the earring the thief takes at midnight

readings.referent: the vibhava ('wealth' or 'unfolding') of the faults of the winds beginning with entering, stolen by the thief, innate joy
the fault of the winds beginning with entering, carried off by the thief, the clear light; with the grasped and the rest absent, the lord of yogis then asks for nothing anywhere in the ten directions

entries.definition: An ascetic who carries a skull-bowl, wears ornaments of bone, keeps to cremation grounds and ignores the rules of caste purity; the observance is found in Śaiva and Buddhist tantric circles alike. Kāṇha calls himself one and puts on a garland of bones for Ḍombī.

'Action seal': in the yoginī tantras, a physical woman partner in the yoga of sexual union, as distinct from an imagined partner and from Mahāmudrā. Munidatta says conventional bodhicitta is 'milked' through the sequence of joys in the course of union with a karmamudrā (cp.02.m2).

Compassion: the wish that beings be free of suffering, paired in Mahāyāna and tantric thought with wisdom. Munidatta says Virūpa speaks with a mind moved again and again by supreme compassion (cp.03.m1); the Sekoddeśa verse he quotes speaks of the lord's strength of wisdom and compassion (cp.03.m5).
An oar, or perhaps a steering paddle, of a boat. In this song there are five of them; what exactly is done with them in the line is uncertain.

symbolic.image: five oars

readings.referent: the instruction of the Five Stages (pañcakrama), which the yogī takes up

entries.definition: A key (Sanskrit kuñcikā, Old Bengali koñcā). In song 4 key and lock are put in the mother-in-law's house. The Tibetan translation has lde kyog, 'hooked key', both in the line and in Munidatta's comment.

symbolic.image: the key put, with the lock, in the mother-in-law's house

readings.referent: with the lock: closing the lock, explained as blocking the door of the root of the jewel (maṇimūla)

entries.definition: The afflictions: disturbing mental states such as desire, hatred and delusion that keep beings in saṃsāra. In the Guhyasamāja verse Munidatta quotes, nirvāṇa is the state that removes all afflictions, reached only with the vajra guru (cp.01.m3).

Throwing or casting (Sanskrit kṣepa; Old Bengali khem̐pa-, here an imperative). In song 4 the yoginī is told to throw; what she throws is not said. The Tibetan translation has 'phangs nas, ‘having thrown’, in the song and the comment. Munidatta takes the throw as union in her own place (svasthānayoga).

symbolic.image: the yoginī told to throw

readings.referent: union in her own place (svasthānayoga), from which she, the Nairātmā yoginī in the form of bodhicitta, enjoys play at the root of the jewel and rises to be absorbed into the wheel of great bliss

entries.definition: The bank or shore of a river (Sanskrit kūla; the manuscript writes kula). The last line has someone sinking at the shore, or 'shore after shore'. The spelling coincides with kula, 'family, clan', a different word that needs its own entry.

symbolic.image: the river bank at which those who climbed into the chariot sink

readings.referent: the body (śarīra), in which yogis proud of outer treatises, not knowing selflessness, wander

entries.definition: In yoga, holding the breath after drawing it in, named from kumbha, 'pot', since the body is held full like a jar. Munidatta speaks of the absorption (samādhi) of kumbhaka purified by vilakṣaṇa and reads the song's crocodile (kumbhīra) through it (cp.02.m2); the Tibetan transcribes the word.

A word the tantras use for the sexual union of yogic practice, usually spelled kunduru; in ordinary Sanskrit kunduru is olibanum, a fragrant resin. The poet calls himself a hero in kundura. Munidatta explains it as the imperishable bliss of uniting the two organs (cp.04.m6); the Tibetan translation keeps the word.

symbolic.image: kundura, in which the poet says he is a hero

readings.referent: the union of the two organs (dvīndriyasamāpatti) and the imperishable bliss of that yoga, by which he crushes the enemy, the afflictions

entries.definition: A lake or large pond, typically one where lotuses grow. In this song Ḍombī breaks the lake and eats the lotus root.

symbolic.image: the lake that Ḍombī breaks

readings.referent: the body, as a lotus pool (kāyapuṣkara)

entries.definition: In tantric yoga, one of the three main channels of the subtle body, usually described as running to the left of the central channel (avadhūtī). Munidatta names lalanā, rasanā and avadhūtikā as the three channels that are pressed and made free of appearance (cp.04.m2).

A lock (compare Bengali tālā); the word tāla also means palm tree and musical time. In song 4 key and lock are put in the mother-in-law's house; in Kāṇha's verse quoted by Munidatta a firm lock is set at the door of the sky (cp.04.m5). The Tibetan translation of the line has lde mig, usually 'key'.

symbolic.image: the lock put, with the key, in the mother-in-law's house

readings.referent: sealing the lock shut (tālasampuṭīkaraṇa), explained as blocking the door of the root of the jewel (maṇimūla)

entries.definition: The water flower that rises unstained from the mud, a pervasive image in Indian religious poetry. In this song there is one lotus with sixty-four petals, on which Ḍombī climbs and dances.

symbolic.image: one lotus with sixty-four petals

readings.referent: the wheel of emanation (nirmāṇacakra), which has sixty-four petals

entries.definition: The edible root and stalk of the lotus (Sanskrit mṛṇāla), gathered from the bed of a pond. In this song Ḍombī breaks the lake and eats it.

symbolic.image: the lotus root that Ḍombī eats

readings.referent: bodhicitta, which in its conventional aspect has the form of semen (he calls it the lake's ‘root’, mūla)

entries.definition: ‘The middle one’ (madhyamā): a name for the central channel of the subtle body, which runs between the left and right channels and which the tantras also call avadhūtī. Munidatta says the moon and the sun, left and right, are joined and made to enter the middle one (cp.03.m2).

forms.where: standard Tibetan equivalent; not checked against toh2293

entries.definition: ‘Great Seal’: in the yoginī tantras, the highest accomplishment (siddhi), the realization of the nature of mind and reality. Munidatta has Kāṇha say that through union with Nairātmā he attains the accomplishment of Mahāmudrā, whose nature is wisdom and means.

Great passion (mahārāga): desire not suppressed but taken up as the means of awakening; it gives its name to what Munidatta calls the way of great passion. He speaks of the sign of the delight of the bliss of great passion seen at Vairocana's door (cp.03.m4) and, in the Tibetan, of the blazing fire of great passion (cp.03.m6).

Munidatta's name for the path of the songs, in which passion is itself the means of freedom rather than something to be suppressed by austerity. He contrasts it with ascetic observances and cites the Hevajra: the world is bound by passion and freed by passion itself (cp.01.m4).

Great bliss: the highest bliss, which the tantric path of the songs takes as its goal. Munidatta equates it with the fourth joy and speaks of the great bliss of innate joy, to be known day and night after questioning the guru (cp.01.m3).

In the yoginī-tantra map of the subtle body, the highest of the four wheels (cakra), at the crown of the head, pictured as a lotus of thirty-two petals. Munidatta identifies Ḍombī's hut outside the town with it.

A circle or disc; in the tantras, the circular arrangement of a deity with its retinue and palace, and by extension a bounded sphere of practice or of the body. In a caryā verse Munidatta quotes, there is no difference among the three maṇḍalas (cp.07.m4); the three are not named.

A word of uncertain sense in song 4: where the yoginī flows before reaching Oḍḍiyāna. Maṇi is 'jewel'; kula may be 'family' or, as elsewhere in the songs, kūla, 'bank'. The Tibetan translation has ma Ni kuN+Da li, perhaps from a different reading. Munidatta's paraphrase has the root of the jewel (maṇimūla) in its place.

symbolic.image: the maṇikula through which the yoginī flows

readings.referent: the root of the jewel (maṇimūla), from which, having enjoyed the taste of play, she rises up and up to the wheel of great bliss (his paraphrase puts maṇimūla where the song has maṇikula; he gives no explicit gloss)

entries.definition: ‘Root of the jewel’: a point in the lower body named in the code language of the yoginī tantras, where the ‘jewel’ (maṇi) usually stands for the male organ. Munidatta says bodhicitta goes to the kacchikā, the root of the jewel, and, opened by innate joy, is to be rowed by way of the wheels (cp.14.m4).

The range or field of the mind (Sanskrit manogocara; Tibetan yid kyi spyod yul): whatever thought can reach. In the refrain of song 7 whatever lies within it is uāsa, 'indifferent'. Munidatta applies the word to yogins in whom understanding through the mind-sense predominates, and quotes Saraha on a place where mind and wind do not move (cp.07.m3).

symbolic.image: whatever lies within the mind's range

readings.referent: yogins who stay within the mind's range, in whom understanding through the mind-sense predominates; they too stand indifferent to this teaching, far removed from it

entries.definition: A woman of the Mātaṅga, a community ranked outside caste society, comparable to the Ḍom. In this song she is the one who ferries across, between the Gaṅgā and the Yamunā. The word can also mean a female elephant, a sense that does not seem to be meant here.

symbolic.image: an outcaste woman who ferries people across the river

entries.definition: Mātsarya: selfish possessiveness, envy or avarice; Buddhist lists of secondary afflictions count it as avarice, the Tibetan ser sna. Munidatta says the mind-deer, restless through the faults of ignorance and avarice that it has itself made, is the sworn enemy of all (cp.06.m3).

Delusion or bewilderment (moha): with desire and hatred, one of the three root afflictions of Buddhist teaching, the confusion that hides how things are. Munidatta speaks of the stain of delusion (mohamala) in describing the yoginī (cp.04.m4); the Tibetan has rmongs pa.

The tree of delusion (moha), which in song 5 is split so that its planks can be joined into the bridge. The Tibetan translation has 'tree of ignorance' (ma rig ljon shing), both in the line and in Munidatta's comment.

symbolic.image: a tree of delusion, split for the planks of the bridge

readings.referent: the tree of conventional bodhicitta, split so as to cut off its grasping of sense objects; the gloss first sets the tree of delusion beside the sense object (viṣaya), and its syntax is loose

entries.definition: The moon. In song 14 the moon and the sun are the two wheels; in the commentary on song 1 Munidatta speaks of the moon of conventional bodhicitta, which Rāhu swallows.

symbolic.image: the moon

readings.referent: conventional bodhicitta
the knowledge of wisdom (prajñājñāna)
with the sun and the pulinda, one of three 'appearances' (ābhāsa) that bring about the making and unmaking of saṃsāra, which practice brings to a stop

entries.definition: Death as Māra, the 'killer' and tempter of Buddhist myth; one of the four Māras, with those of the aggregates, the afflictions and the divine son. Munidatta says that from beginningless time, through lack of vigilance, 'my mind-deer', wrapped in the poison of the Māra of death, heard the cry 'kill! kill!' (māra māra) (cp.06.m2).

A fool, someone deluded (Old Bengali mūṛha, Sanskrit mūḍha). In the last line Bhusuku says it does not enter the hearts of fools. Munidatta identifies them with scholars proud of outer treatises and scriptures, who are thoroughly deluded about this teaching and far from it (cp.06.m6). The Tibetan translation has blun, 'fool'.

symbolic.image: fools, into whose hearts it does not enter

readings.referent: scholars (paṇḍita) proud of outer treatises and scriptures, thoroughly deluded about this teaching and far from it, in whose hearts not even a glimmer of reality opens

entries.definition: A channel of the subtle body. In tantric yoga the vital winds move through a network of channels, of which the chief three are lalanā, rasanā and the central avadhūtī. Munidatta speaks of pressing these three (cp.04.m2).

forms.where: standard Tibetan name of the goddess; not checked against toh2293

entries.definition: Selflessness, the absence of an inherent self in persons and phenomena, personified in the Hevajra tradition as a goddess, Nairātmā, ‘She who is without self’. Munidatta uses the word both for the goddess, whom he addresses in place of Ḍombī, and for selflessness as a doctrine.

Selflessness: the absence of a self. Munidatta uses the term in glossing lines 4a-4b of song 1, and quotes a verse in which the vajra of realizing selflessness splits the mountains of the view of a real self (cp.01.m5). The Hevajra tradition personifies it as the goddess Nairātmyā.

Lacking intrinsic nature (svabhāva): the Madhyamaka teaching that nothing exists by its own nature, another way of stating emptiness. Munidatta opens his comment on song 4 by saying that Guṇḍarīpāda, through understanding the conduct of Heruka, teaches others that things are without intrinsic nature (cp.04.m1).

'Without añjana' (eye-black, hence stain): in siddha and dohā poetry, the unstained, unconditioned state of mind. In the verse of Kṛṣṇācārya that Munidatta quotes, hardly one in ten million becomes absorbed in the stainless (cp.02.m6). The Tibetan translates literally, 'without eye-salve'.

Free of revulsion: untroubled by the disgust that caste purity attaches to impure people, places and substances. Kāṇha uses the word of himself, and Munidatta explains it as being free of faults such as shame.

forms.where: standard Tibetan equivalent; not checked against toh2293

entries.definition: In the yoginī-tantra map of the subtle body, the wheel (cakra) at the navel, the lowest of four along the central channel, pictured as a lotus of sixty-four petals. Munidatta identifies the song's lotus with it.

The cessation of suffering and its causes; freedom from saṃsāra. Munidatta quotes the Guhyasamāja: without the vajra guru one cannot reach nirvāṇa, the peaceful, irreversible state that removes all afflictions (cp.01.m3).

The completion stage: the phase of tantric yoga that follows the visualization of the deity and works with the subtle body toward realization. Munidatta cites Āryadeva: its awakening cannot be realized without passing through the five stages in order (cp.01.m2).

A noose or snare (Sanskrit pāśa), used to catch and bind, and in tantric art an emblem held by deities. In song 1, on this draft's reading of pāsa, the listener is told to take up the noose; the Tibetan translation reads 'noose' (zhags pa) there, and Munidatta's gloss mentions it (cp.01.m5).

symbolic.image: a noose, taken up on the side of emptiness

readings.referent: the nature of selflessness (nairātmadharma), which the listener is to embrace closely; the Tibetan translation of the comment says 'the dharma of selflessness is the noose' (the division of the Sanskrit is uncertain)

entries.definition: Teacher whom Munidatta quotes as saying that the awakening of the completion stage cannot be realized without passing through the five stages in order (cp.01.m2). Tantric tradition places an Āryadeva in the Guhyasamāja lineage as a disciple of Nāgārjuna.

'The Blessed One', a common epithet of the Buddha, used in the tantras also of the buddha who teaches them. Munidatta speaks of the Blessed One's five stages (cp.01.m2) and of the countless absorptions the Blessed One taught (cp.01.m4).

Bhusukupāda, the siddha to whom the manuscript and the Tibetan translation attribute song 6. He names himself Bhusuku in its last couplet, and Munidatta and the Tibetan also read his name in the refrain, where Shastri's text has bhukua. Munidatta calls him a siddha master (cp.06.m6). Shastri's edition identifies him with Śāntideva, whose Bodhicaryāvatāra Munidatta quotes here (cp.06.m3).

Cāṭilapāda, the siddha to whom the manuscript attributes song 5. He names himself Cāṭila in its refrain, where he builds a bridge, and in its last couplet. The commentary also spells the name Cāṭilla; the Tibetan translation has tsA TI la and tsA TI li pa. Munidatta calls him a siddhācārya (cp.05.m3).

Ḍombīpāda, the siddha to whom the manuscript attributes this song. Munidatta introduces him as the siddhācārya Ḍombī, steeped in supreme compassion, who sets out the teaching under the guise of a boat journey. The name is the word for a Ḍom woman with the honorific -pāda.

Guṇḍarīpāda, the siddha to whom the manuscript attributes song 4. He names himself Guḍarī in its last couplet; the manuscript also spells the name Guṇḍarī and Guḍḍarī, and the Tibetan translation guN+Da rI. Munidatta calls him a siddha master who has directly realized the vajra-like samādhi (cp.04.m6).

forms.where: standard Tibetan transcription; not checked against toh2293

entries.definition: A wrathful tantric deity, and a title of Hevajra and related male deities of the yoginī tantras. In the Hevajra Tantra verse Munidatta quotes, the practitioner is told to dance in Heruka's form.

'Victor', a title of a buddha as one who has conquered the afflictions (the Jains use it of their teachers). Munidatta calls the unity of self-blessing and clear light the bridge of the Jina, for carrying beings across the ocean of saṃsāra (cp.05.m5); the Tibetan translation has no word for 'Jina' there.

forms.where: standard Tibetan name for Kṛṣṇācārya; not checked against toh2293

forms.translit: nag po spyod pa pa'i zhabs

entries.definition: Siddha poet, called Kṛṣṇācārya in Sanskrit, to whom songs of this collection are attributed. Munidatta quotes a verse of his in which the pure water dries up when the fire of time (kālāgni) enters (cp.01.m2).

Siddha poet to whom song 2 is attributed; he names himself in its last couplet. The name joins kukkurī, 'female dog', with the honorific -pāda. Munidatta introduces him as setting out the king of great bliss in twilight language, his mind delighted by drinking the liquor of his own bliss (cp.02.m1).

Siddha poet of eastern India to whom song 1 is attributed; he names himself in its refrain and last couplet. Munidatta names him first among the siddhas who composed the songs (cp.01.m1) and calls him 'the first siddha master', ādisiddhācārya (cp.01.m6).

Teacher to whom Munidatta attributes a verse on vajra recitation (vajrajāpa): one who falls from a mountaintop falls though unwilling, and one who has the guru's instruction is freed though not seeking freedom (cp.01.m3). Tantric tradition credits a Nāgārjuna with Guhyasamāja works; whether he is the Madhyamaka philosopher is disputed.

In Indian myth, the demon who swallows the sun or moon and so causes eclipses. Munidatta identifies the Kāla of song 1 with Rāhu, who from the first day of the dark fortnight dries up the moon of conventional bodhicitta through the sequence of lunar days (cp.01.m2).

Siddha poet famous for his dohās, rhymed couplet songs. Munidatta quotes him praising the true guru (cp.01.m3) and asking how the tender sprout of mind, if not watered with the pure juices of sense objects, could become the wish-granting tree (cp.01.m4).

‘The Illuminator’, one of the five buddhas who head the families of tantric deities, often placed at the centre of the maṇḍala. Munidatta calls the tenth door of song 3 ‘the door of Vairocana’ (vairocanadvāra), where the sign of the bliss of great passion is seen (cp.03.m4); he does not say where in the body it lies.
'Vajra being', a buddha form central to many tantric systems. Munidatta ends his comment on song 1 with a verse from the Dvikalpa: the union of āli and kāli is Vajrasattva's seat (cp.01.m6).

Siddha poet to whom song 3 is attributed; he names himself Biruā in its last couplet, and the manuscript heads the song ‘of Virūpāda’. Munidatta calls him Viruāpāda and says he spoke out of supreme compassion to make the avadhūtī plain (cp.03.m1). Tibetan tradition counts a Virūpa among the eighty-four siddhas.

Munidatta's word for a couplet of a song, used when he turns to comment on it ('with the next verse', 'the third verse'). In song 1 he calls couplets 4 and 5 the third and fourth, so he counts the opening couplet as the first and leaves the refrain out of the count.

Wing, side or flank (Sanskrit pakṣa, Old Bengali pakhā); also half of a lunar month, and a party in a dispute. In song 4 the sides of the braid of moon and sun are to be split; the Tibetan translation renders the word there as sgo glegs, 'door-panel'. Munidatta speaks of the 'taking of sides' (pakṣagraha).

symbolic.image: the sides of the braid of moon and sun, which are to be split

readings.referent: the taking of sides (pakṣagraha) by the moon and the sun, which the lord of yogis breaks through the instruction in vajra recitation, so steadying the vajra of speech

entries.definition: A graded sequence of five stages of tantric yoga, associated with the Guhyasamāja tradition and with a work of the same name. Munidatta says those who seek innate joy through the Blessed One's five stages realize the vajra-like absorption, and cites Āryadeva: without them completion-stage awakening cannot be realized (cp.01.m2).

The far bank of a river, used in the phrase pāra kar-, 'take across, ferry over'. Crossing to the far shore is a widespread Buddhist image; Munidatta places the crossing in this song on the ocean of saṃsāra.

symbolic.image: ferrying someone over to the far bank

readings.referent: crossing the ocean of saṃsāra (cp.14.m2), the sea of becoming (cp.14.m6)

entries.definition: The ultimate (paramārtha): how things really are, as against the conventional (saṃvṛti); together they are the two truths. In the verse of Kṛṣṇācārya that Munidatta quotes, people swell with pride, thinking themselves skilled in the ultimate (cp.02.m6).

Goods spread out for sale, or the stall that displays them (Sanskrit prasāra, ‘spreading out’). In song 3 the liquor-seller sets out her wares in sixty-four pots. The Tibetan translation has stegs bu, ‘platform, stall’.

symbolic.image: the wares, or stall, that the liquor-seller sets out

readings.referent: a seat (gdan), apparently the wheel of emanation itself, into which the gandharva being enters from the blazing fire of great passion; the stall (stegs bu) is called twilight language here (the comment survives only in the Tibetan translation)

entries.definition: Paṭamañjarī, the name of the rāga (melodic mode) to which song 1 is sung, given in its heading and repeated at the start of Munidatta's comment (cp.01.m2).

The piṭā of the first line of song 2, which cannot hold, or be held. Munidatta renders it pīṭhaka, 'little seat, stool', and the Tibetan translation stegs bu, 'stand, platform'; both point to a seat or stand rather than a vessel. The syntax of the line, and so the object's role in the milking, is uncertain.

symbolic.image: the stool (or stand) in the milking scene

readings.referent: the vajra jewel (vajramaṇi): conventional bodhicitta falling into it cannot be held, and novice yogis are unable to hold it

entries.definition: The Ganges, the chief river of northern India, sacred in Indian religion. In this song a boat moves between the Gaṅgā and the Yamunā, the two rivers that meet at Prayāga.

symbolic.image: the river Gaṅgā, one of the two rivers the boat moves between

readings.referent: together with the Yamunā, the 'moon-appearance' and the 'sun-appearance' (candrābhāsa, sūryābhāsa), which are the grasped object and the grasping subject; pairing the Gaṅgā with the moon and the grasped follows word order only

entries.definition: Kāmaru, a vernacular form of Kāmarūpa, the ancient kingdom of the Brahmaputra valley in present-day Assam, known in tantric tradition as a seat of the goddess and a land of adepts. In song 2 the young wife goes there at night; the Tibetan translation transcribes the name.

symbolic.image: Kāmaru, where the young wife goes at night

readings.referent: her own place (svasthāna) in the wheel of great bliss, to which the naturally purified avadhūtī goes of itself, free of concepts

entries.definition: Oḍḍiyāna (also Uḍḍiyāna), a land celebrated in tantric Buddhism as a seat of yoginīs and a source of tantras, usually placed in the Swat valley in the northwest, though some locate it in Orissa. In song 4 the yoginī's course ends there; Munidatta's paraphrase has the wheel of great bliss in its place (cp.04.m4).

symbolic.image: Oḍḍiyāna, where the yoginī's course ends

readings.referent: the wheel of great bliss (mahāsukhacakra), into which she is absorbed (his paraphrase puts it where the song has Oḍḍiyāna; he gives no explicit gloss)

entries.definition: The mountain at the centre of the world in Indian cosmology, also called Meru; tantric texts also locate it within the body. Munidatta says the lord of yogis leads the avadhūtikā to the house of breath, the summit of Sumeru (cp.04.m5).
The Yamunā (Jumna), the great river that joins the Ganges at Prayāga. The song uses the vernacular form Jaunā; Munidatta has the Sanskrit Yamunā.

symbolic.image: the river Yamunā, one of the two rivers the boat moves between

readings.referent: together with the Gaṅgā, the 'moon-appearance' and the 'sun-appearance' (candrābhāsa, sūryābhāsa), which are the grasped object and the grasping subject; pairing the Yamunā with the sun and the grasper follows word order only

entries.definition: A plank or board (Old Bengali paṭi). In song 5 the tree of delusion is split and its planks joined to build the bridge. Munidatta's word is pāṭaka; the Tibetan translation has spang leb, 'plank', in the line and in the comment.

symbolic.image: the planks joined after the tree is split

readings.referent: joined in one with the constant light (satatāloka); the Tibetan translation says 'the constant clear light is the plank'

entries.definition: A pot or jar for liquor. In song 3 sixty-four pots (ghaṛi) hold the liquor-seller's wares, and one pot (ḍulī) has a narrow spout. Old Bengali ghaṛi can also mean a period of about twenty-four minutes, and the Tibetan translation renders it both ways (chu tshod and g+ha ṭā). Munidatta's word is ghaṭī, which he links with ghaṭati, ‘joins’.

symbolic.image: the sixty-four pots of wares, and the one pot with a narrow spout

readings.referent: the one pot with the narrow spout: the avadhūtī, called ghaṭī because it joins (ghaṭati) the two truths, conventional and ultimate, and subtle in form because it stops the two appearances

the sixty-four pots: the sixty-four lotus petals of the wheel of emanation (nirmāṇacakra), for which ghaṭī is twilight language (the comment survives only in the Tibetan translation, and its syntax is loose)

entries.definition: 'Radiant, clear light': in the completion-stage yoga of the tantras, the luminous nature of mind that dawns when the winds and concepts have dissolved. Munidatta calls the thief of the refrain 'the thief, clear light', who carries off the fault of the winds (cp.02.m4).

Wisdom (prajñā): discernment of how things really are, above all insight into emptiness; in the tantras it is paired with means (upāya) and pictured as female. In the Bodhicaryāvatāra verse Munidatta quotes, the flesh is to be freed from the cage of bones with the knife of wisdom (cp.06.m3).

The knowledge arising from wisdom (prajñā) in tantric union; it also names the third empowerment. Munidatta says that at night the naturally purified avadhūtī, through wisdom-knowledge, empowers the five aggregates (cp.02.m5); he names the wisdom-knowledge empowerment in song 1 (cp.01.m3).

forms.where: standard Tibetan equivalent; not checked against toh2293

entries.definition: The pairing of wisdom (prajñā), the understanding of emptiness, with means (upāya), compassionate method. In the yoginī tantras the two are pictured as female and male and their union is the goal. Munidatta describes Mahāmudrā, and the Hevajra Tantra itself, as having the nature of wisdom and means.

Faults belonging to nature (prakṛti), apparently the impurities of the body. Munidatta says the river of existence is deep because of them, since urine, excrement and the like flow out through six openings, and that its two banks are smeared with their mud (cp.05.m2). The Tibetan has rang bzhin gyi skyon.

Elaboration or proliferation (prapañca): the spreading out of the world in concepts and words, and in conduct, outward ritual complexity. Munidatta calls the conduct of song 2 'utterly free of elaboration' (niṣprapañca) (cp.02.m6); the conduct entry notes conduct 'with elaboration' (saprapañca) elsewhere.

A word of uncertain sense in this song, set with 'creation and destruction' after the moon and sun are named as the two wheels. In Sanskrit Pulinda is the name of a forest-dwelling people; what it denotes in the boat scene is unclear, so the source form is kept for now.

symbolic.image: pulinda (literal sense uncertain)

readings.referent: 'the neuter' (napuṃsaka), in twilight language; the phrase 'nondual knowledge' just before it in the gloss may also belong to it
with the moon and the sun, one of three 'appearances' (ābhāsa) that make and unmake saṃsāra

entries.definition: A melodic mode of Indian music. Each song is headed by the rāga to which it is sung; song 1 is in Paṭamañjarī. In the commentary the same word rāga also means 'passion', a different term (see way of great passion).

In tantric yoga, one of the three main channels of the subtle body, usually described as running to the right of the central channel (avadhūtī); the word also means 'tongue'. Munidatta names it with lalanā and avadhūtikā as the three channels that are pressed (cp.04.m2).

A river (Old Bengali ṇaī, Sanskrit nadī). Song 5 opens with the river of existence, deep and swift, muddy on both sides and without footing in the middle; the poet's bridge crosses it. Rivers, their banks and their crossings recur throughout the songs.

symbolic.image: the river of existence, deep and swift, with mud on both sides and no footing in the middle

readings.referent: the three appearances (ābhāsatraya), lalanā, rasanā and the rest, which are to be understood as the river in twilight language because of the depth of its near and far banks; in it the surge of sense objects rises and perishes by day, by night and at twilight
the river of great delusion that is the three appearances, which the yogis wish to cross; the Tibetan translation has rtsa, 'channel', where the Sanskrit has 'river', apparently reading nāḍī for nadī

entries.definition: A road or way (Old Bengali bāṭa). In the first line of song 7 āli and kāli block the road, and seeing it Kāṇha is downcast. The Tibetan translation has lam, 'road, path'.

symbolic.image: the road that āli and kāli block

readings.referent: the path of the avadhūtī (avadhūtīmārga), which Kṛṣṇācārya, having received the instruction in vajra recitation, firmly blocks, unifying by means of āli and kāli; the Tibetan has āli and kāli made one and then held firm and stopped in the avadhūtī's path

entries.definition: A Śabara, one of a forest and hill people of eastern and central India whom caste society treated as outsiders; a Śabara woman, the Śabarī, is a figure of the songs. In the verse of Kṛṣṇācārya's Dohākoṣa that Munidatta quotes, the Śabaras dwell on a high mountain peak (cp.06.m4). The Tibetan renders the word sha ba, 'deer'.

forms.where: standard Tibetan equivalent; not checked against toh2293

entries.definition: The innate: what is inborn and unfabricated, a central idea of the siddhas' songs. Munidatta speaks of 'the fruit, innate joy', in the form of coupled union (cp.01.m2) and of 'the great bliss of innate joy' (cp.01.m3).

forms.translit: lhan cig skyes pa'i dga' ba
lhan cig skyes pa'i dga' bas
forms.lemma: lhan cig skyes pa'i dga' ba

entries.definition: 'Innate joy', one of the four joys of tantric yoga (joy, supreme joy, joy of cessation, innate joy); traditions differ over the order of the last two. Munidatta says bodhicitta is opened by it.

Meditative absorption: a settled, one-pointed state of mind. Song 1 asks what all the samādhis are for. Munidatta explains that the absorptions taught for restraining the senses, like harsh fasting observances, achieve nothing on the way of great passion, because they lack bliss (cp.01.m4).

‘Same taste’ (samarasa): the state in which what seemed separate, such as bliss and emptiness or the partners in union, is known as a single savour; a key word of the siddhas' songs, close to ‘one taste’ (ekarasa). In the Sekoddeśa verse Munidatta quotes, the luminous stream becomes of the same taste with the hosts of Jinas (cp.03.m5).

The commitments a tantric initiate takes on, and by extension the ritual substances bound up with them. Munidatta says the yogin pleases the true guru with an offering of pledge substances before receiving the wisdom-knowledge empowerment (cp.01.m3).

Vigilance (saṃprajanya): watchful awareness of what one's body, speech and mind are doing, a key virtue of the Bodhicaryāvatāra, which Munidatta quotes in this song. He blames its lack (asaṃprajanya) for the plight of 'my mind-deer', wrapped from beginningless time in the poison of the Māra of death (cp.06.m2). The Tibetan has shes bzhin ma yin pa.

The round of birth and death in which beings wander, driven by ignorance and craving. In a verse Munidatta quotes from the Sampuṭodbhava, the Vajra-holder calls the mind itself saṃsāra when it is clouded by concepts, restless as lightning and stained by passion (cp.01.m2).

forms.where: standard Tibetan equivalent; not checked against toh2293

entries.definition: The conventional or relative level of truth, things as they appear and are spoken of, as opposed to the ultimate. Munidatta uses it for the conventional aspect of bodhicitta, which he describes as having the form of semen.

The coded idiom of the songs, in which ordinary images such as an outcaste woman, a boat or a lotus carry a hidden sense disclosed by a teacher. Munidatta says Kāṇha speaks here ‘in the twilight language of the word Ḍombī’. Whether sandhyā ‘twilight’ or sandhā ‘intention’ is meant is debated.

A husband's mother, in the joint household the figure of authority over a young wife. In song 4 key and lock are put in the mother-in-law's house. The Tibetan translation has sgyug mo, 'mother-in-law'.

symbolic.image: the mother-in-law's house, where key and lock are put

readings.referent: the house of breath, the summit of Sumeru, to which the lord of yogis leads the avadhūtikā; his words śvāsam āgāraṃ ('breath', 'house') seem to echo sāsu gharem̐, and the Tibetan has dbugs kyi khyim, 'house of breath'

entries.definition: The two truths of Mahāyāna thought: conventional truth (saṃvṛti), how things appear and function, and ultimate truth, their emptiness. Munidatta pictures beings sunk in an ocean of great delusion about the two truths, whom Lūyī wished to rescue (cp.01.m2).

forms.where: standard Tibetan equivalent; not checked against toh2293

entries.definition: 'Accomplished one': a tantric adept who has gained accomplishment (siddhi). The poets of the songs are siddhas; Munidatta calls Lūyī a siddha master, siddhācārya (cp.01.m2), and 'the first siddha master' (cp.01.m6).

Accomplishment: a power or attainment won through practice, above all the supreme accomplishment of awakening. Munidatta quotes the Rativajra calling bodhicitta 'the treasury of all accomplishments' (cp.01.m2), and the Guhyasamāja on harsh austerities that disturb the mind and so defeat accomplishment (cp.01.m4).

The five aggregates (form, feeling, perception, formations and consciousness) into which Buddhist analysis divides a person. Munidatta reads the five branches of the tree in song 1 as these aggregates, 'beginning with form' (cp.01.m2).

The pair creation (sṛṣṭi) and destruction or withdrawal (saṃhāra): the coming into being and dissolution of a world. In this song the phrase stands beside the pulinda after the moon and sun are named as two wheels; Munidatta says the moon, the sun and the pulinda bring about the creation and destruction of saṃsāra.

Steady, still (Old Bengali thira, Sanskrit sthira): in the siddhas' songs, often the steadiness a yogi gives to mind, breath or vital essence so that it neither wavers nor falls. In song 3 the refrain and the last couplet both speak of making something steady; Munidatta names innate joy (cp.03.m3) and the unfallen bodhicitta (cp.03.m5).

symbolic.image: making something steady (the object is unstated in the song)

readings.referent: innate joy, made steady through the joy of cessation by the grace of the vajra guru
the unfallen bodhicitta, made steady through the channel of semen and moved without waves

entries.definition: Bliss, happiness (sukha). In the tantras the songs draw on, the bliss that arises in yogic union is itself the path, and great bliss (mahāsukha) its goal. Munidatta says the world is pervaded by bliss, as pervader and pervaded (cp.07.m3); the Tibetan has 'great bliss' there.

A channel of the subtle body through which semen, the bodily form of bodhicitta, is said to move. Munidatta apparently gives this name to the avadhūtī here: by it, through the guru's instruction, bodhicitta is made steady and moved without waves (cp.03.m5).

A woman who distils and sells liquor (Sanskrit śuṇḍinī), a trade that caste society ranked low. In song 3 she is one woman in two houses who brews liquor with bark and sets out her wares for customers. The Tibetan translation calls her chang ma, ‘beer woman’.

symbolic.image: a woman who brews and sells liquor, one woman in two houses

readings.referent: the avadhūtī, the central channel (‘she, the avadhūtikā, is the liquor-seller’); in the same gloss the mature yogī joins the moon and the sun, left and right, and makes them enter the middle channel (the syntax is loose)

entries.definition: Emptiness: the absence of intrinsic existence in all things, a central idea of Mahāyāna thought. In song 1 it appears in the Old Bengali compound sunupākha, which Munidatta renders śūnyatāpakṣa, 'the side (or wing) of emptiness' (cp.01.m5).
The sun. In this song the sun and the moon are called 'the two wheels'. The pair recurs throughout the songs.

symbolic.image: the sun, one of 'the two wheels'

readings.referent: with the moon and the pulinda, one of three 'appearances' (ābhāsa) that bring about the making and unmaking of saṃsāra, which practice brings to a stop

entries.definition: ‘Self-blessing’ or self-consecration (svādhiṣṭhāna), also the name of the third of the five stages (pañcakrama) of the Guhyasamāja completion stage. Munidatta says that joining moon and sun in the middle channel makes self-blessing firm (cp.03.m2), and speaks of bodhicitta ‘gone to self-blessing’ (cp.03.m3); he does not explain the term.

One's own form: what a thing really is, as against how it appears. Munidatta glosses Kāṇha's ‘in good faith’ as ‘with an intention set on the true nature’ and quotes the Hevajra: the innate is called the true nature, and the true nature itself is nirvāṇa (cp.10.m5).

‘One's own place’ (svasthāna): a phrase in Munidatta's glosses for the proper seat of the yoginī or avadhūtī. He explains the yoginī's throw in song 4 as union in her own place (cp.04.m4); the Kāmaru entry records her own place in the wheel of great bliss (cp.02.m5).

The tamarind (Old Bengali tentali; Sanskrit tintiḍī or ciñcā), a tree with curved, sour pods. Munidatta likens bodhicitta, the fruit of the body-tree, to a tamarind pod for its crookedness. The Tibetan translation renders it bse yab, a fruit name whose identification is uncertain.

symbolic.image: the tamarind of the tree, which the crocodile eats

readings.referent: bodhicitta, the fruit of the body-tree, crooked like a tamarind pod

entries.definition: Cord or string (Sanskrit tantrī), which Ḍombī sells in song 10. Whether cord, an instrument string, thread or even a loom is meant is uncertain.

symbolic.image: the cord that Ḍombī sells

readings.referent: the bhaga (female organ), 'the place of the lotus', which has the form of ignorance

entries.definition: 'Finest of trees', from taru, tree, and vara, excellent. Song 1 opens by calling the body such a tree, with five branches. Munidatta defends the comparison as a poetic figure (utprekṣā) that states a likeness resting on some difference (cp.01.m2).

symbolic.image: a fine tree with five branches

readings.referent: the five aggregates, beginning with form, as the five branches
the six senses, the elements and the sense objects, taken together as the body-tree, its leaves being the grasped, the grasper and the grasping

forms.where: standard Tibetan equivalent; not checked against toh2293

entries.definition: ‘Thus-gone’: an epithet of a buddha. The tantras arrange their deities in families headed by five or six tathāgatas, and Munidatta links six tathāgatas with the wheel, earrings, necklace and other ornaments of tantric conduct.

Reality, 'thatness' (tattva): things as they truly are, which the path aims to know directly. Munidatta says that in the hearts of scholars proud of outer treatises not even a glimmer of reality opens, and quotes a tantra: for those who do not know reality, the Sage's eighty-four thousand heaps of Dharma bear no fruit (cp.06.m6).

Footing, or a bottom within reach in deep water (Old Bengali thāha; compare Hindi thāh, 'bottom', and Bengali athai, 'bottomless'). In song 5 the river of existence has none in the middle. Munidatta repeats the word without a Sanskrit equivalent; the Tibetan translation has 'no place to stay' ('dug gnas med).

symbolic.image: the middle of the river, where there is no footing

readings.referent: the avadhūtī, whose measure (pramāṇa) a novice yogi cannot take

entries.definition: A thief, who in the refrain of song 2 takes the earring at midnight while the household sleeps. The refrain's cauri may be the agent case or a feminine, 'thief-woman'; the Tibetan rkun ma does not decide it. Munidatta names the thief differently in two comments.

symbolic.image: the thief who takes the earring at midnight

readings.referent: innate joy (sahajānanda), the thief who steals the 'wealth' of the faults of the winds
the clear light (prabhāsvara), the thief who carries off the fault of the winds

entries.definition: A word of uncertain sense in the first line of song 4: the thing the yoginī is asked to press. Its first part is probably ti-, 'three'. Munidatta cites it as tiyaṛa; the Tibetan translation has ka mgo, whose sense here is unclear.

symbolic.image: the tiaḍḍā that the yoginī is asked to press

readings.referent: the three channels, lalanā, rasanā and avadhūtikā, which are pressed and made free of appearance

entries.definition: 'Ford-maker': a follower of a non-Buddhist religious path. In the Hevajra verse Munidatta quotes, buddhatīrthika most likely means 'Buddhists and tīrthikas', those who do not know the reversed meditation in which passion frees (cp.01.m4).

A tortoise: the Old Bengali duli, which the Tibetan translation renders rus sbal. Song 2 opens with the paradox of milking one. Munidatta's gloss echoes the word's syllables (dvaya, 'dual'; līna, 'dissolved'), a division the Tibetan commentary spells out.

symbolic.image: a tortoise that is milked

readings.referent: the lotus of great bliss (mahāsukhakamala), in which the dual aspect has dissolved; duli is to be understood in the convention of twilight language
its milking: conventional bodhicitta, drawn out through the sequence of joys beginning with joy in the course of union with a karmamudrā, which travels the path of the avadhūtī

entries.definition: A town or city, the settled world of caste society. Untouchable communities such as the Ḍoms lived outside it, and in this song Ḍombī's hut stands beyond it.

symbolic.image: the town, outside which Ḍombī's hut stands

readings.referent: the mass of sense objects, beginning with visible form

entries.definition: The three worlds or realms into which Buddhist cosmology divides saṃsāra: the realm of desire, the realm of form and the formless realm; also used loosely for the whole world. Munidatta says the avadhūtī, in its conventional aspect as semen, creates the three worlds (cp.02.m5).

A tree (Old Bengali rukha, from Sanskrit vṛkṣa). In song 2 a crocodile eats the tamarind of the tree. The plain word is distinct from taruvara, 'fine tree', in song 1, though Munidatta reads both trees as the body.

symbolic.image: the tree whose tamarind the crocodile eats

readings.referent: the body, as 'the body-tree' (kāyavṛkṣa), whose fruit is bodhicitta

entries.definition: The vajra of body, of speech and of mind: a buddha's body, speech and mind, which tantric practice aims to make the practitioner's own. Munidatta says the lord of yogis first makes the vajra of body firm through deity yoga, steadies the vajra of speech by vajra recitation, then works to make the vajra of mind firm (cp.04.m5).

forms.translit: byang chub sems dpa'i spyod pa la 'jug pa
forms.lemma: byang chub sems dpa'i spyod pa la 'jug pa

entries.definition: The Bodhicaryāvatāra ('Entering the Conduct of Awakening'), Śāntideva's verse treatise on the bodhisattva path. Munidatta quotes its verses on separating skin, flesh and bones with the knife of wisdom and asking what core there is in the body (cp.06.m3). The Tibetan translation names it byang chub sems dpa'i spyod pa la 'jug pa.

forms.translit: lha mo bzhis zhus pa rnal 'byor chen po'i rgyud

entries.definition: The Caturdevīparipṛcchā ('Questions of the Four Goddesses'), a mahāyoga tantra usually counted among the explanatory tantras of the Guhyasamāja. Munidatta quotes its verse: for those who do not know reality, the Sage's eighty-four thousand heaps of Dharma bear no fruit (cp.06.m6). The Tibetan has lha mo bzhis zhus pa.

Dohākoṣa ('Treasury of Dohās'), a title given to collections of dohā couplets by several siddhas, among them Saraha and Kāṇha. Here Munidatta quotes the one by Kṛṣṇācārya (Kāṇha): Kāṇha clearly knows the one path of the innate, while those who read and recite the many scriptures know nothing (cp.05.m6).

The Guhyasamāja ('Secret Assembly') Tantra, a major Buddhist tantra, which Munidatta cites as the Śrī Samāja. Here he quotes it on the need for the vajra guru (cp.01.m3) and against harsh austerities, urging that awakening be accomplished through bliss (cp.01.m4).

forms.translit: dpal ldan he ru ka'i rgyud kyi rgyal po

entries.definition: A tantra Munidatta cites as the Śrī Heruka Tantra, for an analysis in which nothing is found, taught in its chapter on reality (tattvapaṭala) (cp.05.m3). Which work is meant is uncertain: Heruka is a name both of Hevajra and of Cakrasaṃvara, so a tantra of either cycle may be intended.

forms.where: standard Tibetan title; not checked against toh2293

entries.definition: The Hevajra Tantra, a major Buddhist yoginī tantra, also called the Dvikalpa after its two parts. Munidatta quotes it on passion: the world is bound by passion and freed by passion itself (cp.01.m4); and on the union of āli and kāli as Vajrasattva's seat (cp.01.m6).

A tantric work that Munidatta cites by the name Rativajra; it is not otherwise identified here. He quotes its verse asking how there can be flawless accomplishment once bodhicitta, the treasury of all accomplishments, has fallen and the consciousness of the aggregates has swooned (cp.01.m2).

forms.translit: lhan cig skyes pa'i sdom pa
forms.lemma: lhan cig skyes pa'i sdom pa

entries.definition: A work Munidatta cites as the Sahajasaṃvara (Tibetan lhan cig skyes pa'i sdom pa); it is not otherwise identified here. He quotes its verse in which emptiness, like a woman in desire, at once embraces the mind that is all-pervading, free of appearance and of one taste with compassion (cp.06.m5).

A Buddhist tantra, cited by Munidatta as 'the king of tantras, Sampuṭodbhava', probably the Saṃpuṭa Tantra of the Hevajra and Cakrasaṃvara traditions. He quotes its verse in which the Vajra-holder calls the mind, clouded by concepts and restless as windblown lightning, saṃsāra (cp.01.m2).
