The Sekoddeśa (‘Summary of Empowerment’), a work of the Kālacakra tradition on tantric empowerment. Munidatta quotes from it a verse on the luminous stream of the moon that must not fall, and on knowing the innate form of the lord (cp.03.m5). The Tibetan translation names it dbang bshad pa.

forms.translit: rnal 'byor rin po che'i phreng ba
forms.lemma: rnal 'byor rin po che'i phreng ba

entries.definition: The Yogaratnamālā (‘Garland of Yoga Jewels’), probably the commentary on the Hevajra Tantra of that name ascribed to Kṛṣṇa (Kāṇha). Munidatta quotes from it a verse calling emptiness the vajra: firm, solid, not hollow, uncuttable, unbreakable, unburnable and indestructible (cp.03.m3).

Indifferent, standing apart (Sanskrit udāsa, udāsīna; the Old Bengali uāsa drops the d, as Prakrit regularly does between vowels). In the refrain of song 7 whatever lies in the mind's range is uāsa. Munidatta adds sudūratara, 'very far removed' (cp.07.m3); the Tibetan has btang snyoms, 'equanimity, indifference', in the song and the commentary.

Instruction: the practical, often oral, teaching a guru gives a disciple for yogic practice. Munidatta quotes Nāgārjuna on helpful instruction gained by the guru's grace (cp.01.m3), and says Lūyī saw coupled union by practising the fourth instruction received from the guru (cp.01.m6).

The protuberance on the crown of a buddha's head, one of the marks of a great being; tantric accounts of the body also use the word for the top of the head. Munidatta speaks of the honey of the uṣṇīṣa lotus (cp.04.m3).

The generation stage: the first phase of tantric practice, in which practitioners visualize themselves as the deity with its maṇḍala, in preparation for the completion stage. In the verse Munidatta attributes to Nāgārjuna, a means built like a stairway serves those established in the generation stage who long for the completion stage (cp.07.m6).

The thunderbolt-diamond, emblem of the indestructible in tantric Buddhism; as a prefix it marks what belongs to that path (vajra guru, vajra recitation). Munidatta uses vajra and its synonym kuliśa, as in 'the union of vajra and lotus' (cp.01.m3) and 'the vajra of realizing selflessness' (cp.01.m5).

A breathing practice of the completion stage, associated with the Guhyasamāja and the Five Stages, usually described as joining the syllables oṃ āḥ hūṃ to the breath as it enters, abides and leaves. Munidatta says the lord of yogis is first to lead both into the house by instruction in vajra recitation (cp.02.m3).

'Vajra jewel': in the code language of the yoginī tantras, the tip of the male organ (vajra and maṇi, 'jewel', both stand for it). Munidatta equates the song's stool (pīṭhaka) with it: conventional bodhicitta falling into it cannot be held, and novice yogis cannot hold it (cp.02.m2).

forms.translit: rdo rje lta bu'i ting nge 'dzin
forms.lemma: rdo rje lta bu'i ting nge 'dzin

entries.definition: In Mahāyāna accounts of the path, the final meditative absorption, which like a vajra cuts through the last and subtlest obscurations just before awakening. Munidatta says Guḍḍarī speaks his own praise because he has directly realized it (cp.04.m6).

Left and right, the two sides. In song 5 whoever climbs onto the bridge is told not to go right or left. Munidatta pairs left and right with the moon and the sun, here with their 'appearances' (cp.05.m5), and calls the river's two banks left and right (cp.05.m2).

symbolic.image: going right or left on the bridge

readings.referent: the moon-appearance and the sun-appearance (candrasūryābhāsa), left and right, which are first stopped by vajra recitation and are then not to be dwelt on again (the sense of the instruction is not fully clear)

entries.definition: Vāruṇī, a strong distilled liquor named after the god Varuṇa; Vāruṇī is also the goddess of wine. In song 3 the liquor-seller brews it, and it returns in the refrain. The Tibetan translation renders it chu bdag chang, ‘Varuṇa's beer’, or simply chang, ‘beer’.

symbolic.image: the liquor the liquor-seller brews

readings.referent: bodhicitta, which she binds, ‘because of the delight of bliss’
conventional bodhicitta: Munidatta calls vāruṇī a twilight word (sandhyāvacana) for it

entries.definition: Wind or breath (Sanskrit vāyu, vāta, pavana, prāṇa; Old Bengali pavaṇa; Tibetan rlung): in tantric yoga, the vital winds that move through the channels of the subtle body and carry the mind; stilling them is a central aim. Munidatta speaks of the winds beginning with entering, and of the wind of emergence.

A braid or plait of hair (Sanskrit veṇī); the same word names the meeting of rivers, as at the Triveṇī of Prayāga. In song 4 the moon and the sun form a braid whose sides are to be split. The Tibetan translation has gnyis, 'the two', where the Bengali has beṇi.

symbolic.image: a braid made of the moon and the sun

entries.definition: 'Variety': in the Hevajra system, the first of the four moments (kṣaṇa) of yogic union, followed by vipāka, vimarda and vilakṣaṇa. Munidatta says the yoginī gives the sequence of joys through union with the characteristics beginning with vicitra (cp.04.m2).

Evening (Sanskrit vikāla, Old Bengali biālī), the time the poet names for the rubbing of lotus and vajra. Munidatta takes the word as vi-kāla, 'without time'. The Tibetan translation gives both dus min, 'not the time', and dgongs mo, 'evening'.

symbolic.image: evening, the time named for the rubbing of lotus and vajra

readings.referent: free of time (kālarahita): the yogi is told to realize directly the accomplishment of Mahāmudrā, which is free of time

entries.definition: Conceptual thought (vikalpa, kalpanā): the mind's construction of things through concepts, which Buddhist tantric teaching treats as what binds. Munidatta speaks of shaking off the concepts of beginningless existence, of going to the wheel of great bliss free of concepts (nirvikalpa), and of the innate wind freed from the net of concepts (cp.02.m4, cp.02.m5).

‘Beyond characteristics’: in the Hevajra system, the last of the four moments (kṣaṇa) of yogic union, commonly paired with innate joy, though systems differ. Munidatta twice speaks of something ‘purified by vilakṣaṇa’: the boat or the avadhūtī (cp.14.m2), and the bodhicitta that is rowed as a boat (cp.14.m5).

Downcast, dejected (Old Bengali bimana, Sanskrit vimanas, literally 'without mind' or 'of altered mind'). Twice in song 7 Kāṇha becomes bimana. The Tibetan translation of the song takes it as unhappiness (rnam mi dga', yid mi bde); Munidatta's paraphrase, in the Sanskrit and the Tibetan alike, has 'of distinguished mind' (viśiṣṭamanas) in its place.

symbolic.image: Kāṇha becoming bimana: downcast, or literally 'without mind'

readings.referent: becoming of distinguished mind (viśiṣṭamanas): having unified by means of āli and kāli and firmly blocked the path of the avadhūtī, Kṛṣṇācārya, by the true guru's grace, becomes of distinguished mind in the form of the naturally purified avadhūtikā (the paraphrase puts viśiṣṭamanaso bhūtāḥ where the song has bimana bhailā; there is no explicit gloss)
becoming of distinguished mind and purified, through knowing, by the guru's grace, the nature of conventional truth in the arising and perishing of things (again a paraphrase, not an explicit gloss)

entries.definition: Hero; in the yoginī tantras also a title of the male adept, the partner of the yoginīs. The poet of song 4 calls himself a hero in kundura; Munidatta says he is one because he has crushed the enemy, the afflictions (cp.04.m6). The Tibetan translation of the line has no separate word for 'hero'.

One of the four joys (ānanda) that the yoginī tantras describe in yogic union; viramānanda is the ‘joy of cessation’. Its position among the four differs between systems. Munidatta pairs it with the ‘root of the jewel’ (maṇimūla).

The objects of the senses: visible form, sound, smell, taste and touch, with mental objects in some lists. Munidatta reads the town of song 10 as 'the mass of sense objects beginning with form', and speaks of 'the appearance of objects' (viṣayābhāsa).

Emergence or rising (vyutthāna): in yoga, coming out of absorption; in breath practice apparently the outgoing phase of the breath, paired with entering (praveśa). Munidatta reads the courtyard of song 2's refrain as the wind of emergence, together with entering (cp.02.m3); the Tibetan has 'byung ba'i rlung, 'wind of arising'.

A wheel. In this song the moon and the sun are called 'the two wheels', though the vehicle is a boat. The same word (Sanskrit cakra) also names the wheels of the subtle body in the tantras, which have their own entries (wheel of emanation, wheel of great bliss).

symbolic.image: the moon and the sun as 'the two wheels'

entries.definition: A class of powerful spirits of Indian religion, sometimes benign, often feared. In the verse Munidatta quotes, a painter draws a terrifying yakṣa and is then frightened by it himself; so is the fool in saṃsāra (cp.02.m5).

'Yogic sleep': a state of deep meditative rest, outwardly like sleep. Munidatta equates it with the fourth joy and reads the father-in-law's falling asleep as the breath being led into it (cp.02.m4); the Tibetan translation calls it the yogic sleep of 'the joy of peace'.

A practitioner of yoga; in the songs, a tantric adept on the siddhas' path. Kāṇha calls himself a kāpālika yogi, and Munidatta speaks of yogins who lack the guru's lineage. Distinct from 'lord of yogis' (yogīndra), Munidatta's term for the accomplished practitioner.
'Lord of yogis', Munidatta's usual term for the accomplished practitioner the songs speak of; in this song, the one the Ḍombī ferries across.

A woman practitioner of yoga; in the yoginī tantras also a female deity of the maṇḍala. Munidatta says the yoginīs, in the form of the naturally purified avadhūtī, keep awake day and night, glossing the wakeful young wife (cp.02.m4).

'Yoked as a pair': the state in which two poles, such as wisdom and method or the two truths, are inseparably joined. Munidatta says the fruit of innate joy has this form (cp.01.m2) and that Lūyī saw it through practising the fourth instruction received from the guru (cp.01.m6).
